# Conservation of energy for a sphere-valued wave map

## Original exercise

Lawrence C. Evans, *Partial Differential Equations*, second edition,
Graduate Studies in Mathematics 19, AMS, 2010, section 12.6, exercise 14,
printed page 694. The preceding exercise 13 defines the sphere-valued
wave map. ISBN: 978-0-8218-4974-3.

> 14. Prove that if \(\mathbf u\) is a wave map into the unit sphere,
> with compact support in space, we have conservation of energy:
> \[
> \frac{d}{dt}\int_{\mathbb R^n}
>       |\mathbf u_t|^2+|D\mathbf u|^2\,dx=0.
> \]

## Fixed interpretation and complete target

A sphere-valued map cannot vanish outside a compact set. As approved by
the user on 2026-10-23, interpret spatial compact support as compact support
of a perturbation from a **fixed unit vector**, locally uniformly in time.
This is a disclosed nontrivial interpretation, not a claimed author-issued
correction.

Let \(n,m\geq1\) be integers and let
\(u:\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^m\) be jointly smooth.
Fix \(q\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(|q|=1\). Assume:

1. \(|u(x,t)|=1\) for all \(x\) and \(t>0\).
2. The acceleration \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu\) is normal to the sphere at
   \(u\): at each point there is a real scalar \(a(x,t)\) with
   \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu=a u\). No regularity of the selected scalar is
   assumed.
3. For every \(0<s<t<\infty\), a compact set
   \(C_{[s,t]}\subset\mathbb R^n\) exists such that \(u(x,r)=q\) for
   \(x\notin C_{[s,t]}\), \(r\in[s,t]\).

With Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure, define

\[
e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+\sum_{j=1}^n|\partial_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2,
\qquad E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e(x,t)\,dx.
\]

The spatial gradient square is the Frobenius square, and
\(\Delta_xu=\sum_j\partial_{x_jx_j}u\) component by component.
Prove integrability of \(e(\cdot,t)\), differentiability of \(E\),
and \(E'(t)=0\) for every \(t>0\). No assertion at time zero is required.
value.conclusion: For every t>0, e(·,t) is Lebesgue integrable on ℝ^n. The energy E:(0,∞)→ℝ is differentiable and E'(t)=0 for every t>0; consequently E is constant on (0,∞). The energy is exactly ∫_{ℝ^n}(|u_t|²+|Du|²) dx with no factor 1/2. No assertion at time zero is made.

hypotheses.statement: n≥1 and m≥1 are integer dimensions.
hypotheses.origin: problem.md:25; positive integer dimensions represented by natural-number indices with their lower bounds retained here.

hypotheses.statement: For every x∈ℝ^n and t>0 there exists a real scalar a such that u_tt(x,t)−Delta u(x,t)=a u(x,t). No regularity of any selected scalar is assumed.
For every pair of real times 0<s<t<∞ there exists a compact set C_[s,t]⊂ℝ^n such that u(x,r)=q whenever x∉C_[s,t] and r∈[s,t].

definitions.type: Lebesgue measure and integral notation on real coordinate spaces
definitions.definition: For a natural dimension d, dx denotes standard Lebesgue measure on ℝ^d; integrals are Lebesgue integrals. In dimension zero the coordinate space is a singleton of measure one. On coordinate rectangles the measure is the product of the one-dimensional Lebesgue measures. For integrable real functions the integral has its usual real value.

definitions.type: Euclidean and differential notation for the smooth map u
definitions.definition: The dot denotes the Euclidean inner product on ℝ^m, |v| its Euclidean norm with |v|²=v·v. For x∈ℝ^n and t>0, u_t and u_tt are the first and second time derivatives of u; ∂_{x_j}u and ∂_{x_jx_j}u are its coordinate derivatives, for 1≤j≤n, taken component by component. Delta u=Δ_x u=Σ_{j=1}^n ∂_{x_jx_j}u. The spatial gradient square |Du|² is the Frobenius square Σ_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u|². Mixed derivatives use the same componentwise convention.

definitions.definition: For every t>0, E(t)=∫_{ℝ^n}e(x,t) dx, with the Euclidean density e and Lebesgue measure dx specified above.

value.representation_notes: Use one ambient Euclidean representation throughout: Space d = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d) = PiLp 2 (fun _ => ℝ). Its norm and real inner product are the Euclidean ones; PiLp.inner_apply identifies the latter with the coordinate dot product. Fin n labels the original n coordinates by j.val + 1; it introduces neither a missing endpoint nor an extra coordinate. PiLp.single 2 j 1 is the unit vector in coordinate j, so spatial is the Fréchet derivative evaluated on that vector. ut and utt are successive ordinary time derivatives, uxx successive same-coordinate spatial derivatives, and utx is the spatial derivative of ut. Under H002 equality of mixed derivatives identifies utx with the time derivative of ux; proving this identification is part of T004/T007, not a hidden assumption. densityTime is the ACTUAL time derivative of the density, not an assumed product formula. The parameter u is an arbitrary total ambient representative; H002 and all geometric hypotheses concern only positive times. Any source map extends by zero for t≤0, without requiring boundary regularity, and restriction recovers it. Since positive times form an open set, derivatives of all orders and energy germs there depend only on that restriction. No conclusion concerns the chosen exterior values. ContDiffOn uses (∞ : ℕ∞ω), meaning every finite derivative order, not ω (analyticity) or the top element of ℕ∞ω. Header definitions assert no regularity or integrability. The total Bochner integral in energy gains its intended finite Lebesgue meaning only after T003 proves integrability. volume is standard normalized Euclidean Lebesgue measure; EuclideanSpace.volume_preserving_symm_measurableEquiv_toLp identifies it with product coordinate Lebesgue measure. In N002, iteratedFDeriv of positive natural order is the multilinear encoding of all mixed space/time derivatives: evaluation on coordinate unit vectors recovers them, and multilinearity plus the coordinate basis gives the converse. All this is in the same Euclidean representation; local product-coordinate measure transport in T008 is checked inside that obligation. No M ports are retained: the four supplied library theorems are used directly under their actual hypotheses. H003 is preserved although the source proof never needs the norm of q. For measures, ENNReal.ofReal ((2*R)^n) encodes a nonnegative real box volume; R>0 and the explicit non-top clause prevent treating an infinite mass as a real finite integral. Integrable means almost everywhere strong measurability together with finite integral of the norm. The supplied dominated-convergence theorem requires these norm and measurability conditions, not merely pointwise convergence. For the scalar FTC, ℝ supplies completeness; the derivative must exist on the unordered closed interval and its function must be interval integrable. Fubini will be used with finite restricted coordinate measures, hence s-finite, and a genuinely integrable real function. These typeclass capabilities are properties of the chosen standard spaces and measures, not additional hypotheses on the wave map.

steps.statement:
∀ (x : WaveMap.Space n) (t : ℝ), 0 < t →
  inner ℝ (u (x,t)) (WaveMap.ut u x t) = 0 ∧
  inner ℝ (WaveMap.ut u x t) (WaveMap.utt u x t - WaveMap.laplace u x t) = 0 ∧
  inner ℝ (u (x,t)) (WaveMap.utt u x t) = -(‖WaveMap.ut u x t‖ ^ 2) ∧
  (∀ j : Fin n, inner ℝ (u (x,t)) (WaveMap.uxx u j x t) = -(‖WaveMap.ux u j x t‖ ^ 2)) ∧
  (∀ a : ℝ, WaveMap.utt u x t - WaveMap.laplace u x t = a • u (x,t) →
    a = (∑ j, ‖WaveMap.ux u j x t‖ ^ 2) - ‖WaveMap.ut u x t‖ ^ 2) ∧
  WaveMap.utt u x t - WaveMap.laplace u x t =
    ((∑ j, ‖WaveMap.ux u j x t‖ ^ 2) - ‖WaveMap.ut u x t‖ ^ 2) • u (x,t)
steps.explanation: Full N001. Differentiate the unit constraint once and twice in time and in each coordinate on the positive-time open set; dot normality with u and ut. Choose a only pointwise and prove its value for every scalar satisfying normality; never differentiate a.

steps.statement:
∀ t0 : ℝ, 0 < t0 → ∃ (C : Set (WaveMap.Space n)) (R : ℝ),
  IsCompact C ∧ 0 < R ∧ C ⊆ WaveMap.openBox n R ∧
  (∀ x : WaveMap.Space n, x ∉ C → ∀ r ∈ WaveMap.timeInterval t0, u (x,r) = q) ∧
  (∀ (k : ℕ) (x : WaveMap.Space n) (r : ℝ), 0 < k → x ∉ C →
    r ∈ WaveMap.timeInterior t0 → iteratedFDeriv ℝ k u (x,r) = 0)
steps.explanation: Existing common-support subargument. Use J=[t0/2,3t0/2], choose C by H006, enlarge its bound to the open coordinate box, and use local equality with the fixed constant q on the open complement times int J. Establish all positive-order iterated derivatives vanish there; no condition on the norm of q is needed.

steps.statement:
(∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → Integrable (fun x => WaveMap.density u x t)) ∧
  ContDiffOn ℝ (∞ : ℕ∞ω) (fun p => WaveMap.density u p.1 p.2) (WaveMap.positive n) ∧
  ContDiffOn ℝ (∞ : ℕ∞ω) (fun p => WaveMap.densityTime u p.1 p.2) (WaveMap.positive n) ∧
  ∀ t0 : ℝ, 0 < t0 → ∃ (C : Set (WaveMap.Space n)) (R η B : ℝ),
    IsCompact C ∧ 0 < R ∧ 0 < η ∧ 0 ≤ B ∧
    C ⊆ WaveMap.openBox n R ∧ IsCompact (WaveMap.box n R) ∧
    volume (WaveMap.box n R) = ENNReal.ofReal ((2 * R) ^ n) ∧
    volume (WaveMap.box n R) ≠ ⊤ ∧
    Icc (t0 - η) (t0 + η) ⊆ WaveMap.timeInterior t0 ∧
    (∀ x : WaveMap.Space n, x ∉ C → ∀ r ∈ WaveMap.timeInterval t0, u (x,r) = q) ∧
    (∀ (k : ℕ) (x : WaveMap.Space n) (r : ℝ), 0 < k → x ∉ C →
      r ∈ WaveMap.timeInterior t0 → iteratedFDeriv ℝ k u (x,r) = 0) ∧
    (∀ r ∈ WaveMap.timeInterior t0, ∀ (j : Fin n) (f : WaveMap.Space n → ℝ),
      f ∈ WaveMap.terms u r j →
      Continuous f ∧ Function.support f ⊆ C ∧
      (∃ K : ℝ, 0 ≤ K ∧ ∀ x ∈ WaveMap.box n R, |f x| ≤ K) ∧
      Measurable f ∧ Integrable f) ∧
    (∀ x ∈ WaveMap.box n R, ∀ r ∈ Icc (t0 - η) (t0 + η), |WaveMap.densityTime u x r| ≤ B)
steps.explanation: Full N002 with the same common witnesses. Prove smoothness of density and its actual time derivative; continuity, support, measurability, box bounds and absolute integrability for exactly the seven listed terms. The list quantifies every coordinate; H001 supplies a coordinate when extracting the coordinate-independent entries. Coordinate product volume gives (2R)^n and compactness of the box. Set η=t0/4 and bound |e_t| on the compact space-time box to choose B. Keep C,R,η,B jointly quantified. Apply this at an arbitrary positive time to export energy-density integrability separately.

steps.statement:
∀ (x : WaveMap.Space n) (t : ℝ), 0 < t →
  HasDerivAt (WaveMap.density u x) (WaveMap.densityTime u x t) t ∧
  WaveMap.densityTime u x t = 2 * WaveMap.kineticProduct u t x +
    2 * ∑ j, WaveMap.gradientProduct u j t x
steps.explanation: Pointwise product-rule subargument of N003. Derive time differentiability of density from smoothness, identify utx with the time derivative of ux by equality of mixed coordinate derivatives, and compute the exact factor-2 formula. Derivative existence is explicit, since deriv alone defaults to zero when no derivative exists.

steps.statement:
∀ t0 : ℝ, 0 < t0 → ∃ R η B : ℝ,
  0 < R ∧ 0 < η ∧ 0 ≤ B ∧ Icc (t0 - η) (t0 + η) ⊆ Ioi (0 : ℝ) ∧
  Integrable (WaveMap.bound n R B) ∧
  ∀ h : ℝ, 0 < |h| → |h| < η → ∀ x : WaveMap.Space n,
    |WaveMap.quotient u t0 h x| ≤ WaveMap.bound n R B x
steps.explanation: Existing domination subargument. Choose the common witnesses from N002, apply exists_hasDerivAt_eq_slope to density at ordered endpoints min(t0,t0+h), max(t0,t0+h), use the uniform |densityTime|≤B bound, and handle both increment signs. Outside the box both density values vanish. The dominating function is exactly B times the box indicator and is integrable by finite box measure.

steps.statement:
∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t →
  HasDerivAt (WaveMap.energy u) (∫ x, WaveMap.densityTime u x t) t ∧
  (∀ x : WaveMap.Space n, WaveMap.densityTime u x t =
    2 * WaveMap.kineticProduct u t x + 2 * ∑ j, WaveMap.gradientProduct u j t x) ∧
  Integrable (fun x => WaveMap.densityTime u x t) ∧
  Integrable (WaveMap.kineticProduct u t) ∧
  (∀ j : Fin n, Integrable (WaveMap.gradientProduct u j t))
steps.explanation: Full N003. For every nonzero increment sequence in the η-window tending to zero, establish measurability and pointwise convergence of the density quotients using T004, and dominate using T005. Apply MeasureTheory.tendsto_integral_of_dominated_convergence with μ=volume, codomain ℝ, sequence quotient u t0 (h k), limit densityTime, and the box indicator bound. Linearity uses the finite integrals from N002. Pass from all such sequences to the punctured real limit by the source sequential criterion and conclude HasDerivAt of the actual energy integral. Retain the product formula and integrability of every summand.

steps.statement:
∀ (t : ℝ), 0 < t → ∀ j : Fin n,
  ContDiff ℝ (∞ : ℕ∞ω) (WaveMap.flux u j t) ∧ HasCompactSupport (WaveMap.flux u j t) ∧
  (∀ x : WaveMap.Space n, WaveMap.spatial (WaveMap.flux u j t) j x =
    WaveMap.gradientProduct u j t x + WaveMap.laplaceProduct u j t x) ∧
  Integrable (WaveMap.spatial (WaveMap.flux u j t) j) ∧
  Integrable (WaveMap.gradientProduct u j t) ∧ Integrable (WaveMap.laplaceProduct u j t)
steps.explanation: Existing flux subargument of N004. At fixed positive t, smoothness of u yields spatial smoothness of the flux; the compact support in N002 yields HasCompactSupport. Compute its coordinate derivative by the product rule, symmetry of the real inner product, and the definitions. Retain integrability of the derivative and both terms. N002 also supplies the common box for the following FTC/Fubini step.

steps.statement:
∀ (t : ℝ), 0 < t → ∀ j : Fin n,
  (∫ x, WaveMap.gradientProduct u j t x) = -(∫ x, WaveMap.laplaceProduct u j t x) ∧
  Integrable (WaveMap.gradientProduct u j t) ∧ Integrable (WaveMap.laplaceProduct u j t)
steps.explanation: Full N004 using exactly coordinate FTC followed by Fubini. Choose C,R from N002 and a coordinate j. Reindex coordinates into the distinguished real coordinate and the remaining n−1 coordinates, proving the product-Lebesgue transport before using it. The flux vanishes at ±R. Apply intervalIntegral.integral_eq_sub_of_hasDerivAt on each line; continuous derivatives on the closed interval give interval integrability. Apply MeasureTheory.integral_prod to the integrable derivative on the compact box with restricted finite measures, so its integral is zero. Restore the integral on all space by support, integrate T007's product identity, and rearrange finite integrals. Include the n=1 case with a singleton remaining-coordinate space of measure one; no dimension is silently excluded.

steps.statement: ∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → HasDerivAt (WaveMap.energy u) 0 t
steps.explanation: Substitute N003's derivative formula, use N004 coordinate by coordinate, and use finite-sum linearity with N002 integrability to obtain 2 times the integral of inner ut (utt−laplace). N001 makes this integrand zero pointwise. This proves genuine differentiability with zero derivative, not merely a statement about the total deriv operator.

steps.statement:
(∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → Integrable (fun x => WaveMap.density u x t)) ∧
  (∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → HasDerivAt (WaveMap.energy u) 0 t) ∧
  (∀ (s t : ℝ), 0 < s → 0 < t → WaveMap.energy u s = WaveMap.energy u t)
steps.explanation: Full P. Keep density integrability from N002 and HasDerivAt zero from T009. For 0<s<t, apply exists_hasDerivAt_eq_slope to energy with derivative function zero on [s,t], where T009 gives differentiability and hence continuity. Multiply by t−s>0. Order arbitrary positive times or use reflexivity to obtain constancy for every pair. The defined density and energy have exactly the original normalization, without a factor 1/2 or an assertion at time zero.

R001.fact: For a smooth map v from an open subset of ℝ^n×ℝ to ℝ^m, the derivative in any available time or spatial coordinate s satisfies ∂_s(v·v)=2v·∂_s v. If v·v=1 in a neighborhood, this derivative is zero there.

grounds.reason: H002 supplies smoothness of every component of u.
H004 and |u|²=u·u give u·u=1 throughout the domain.
D002 specifies Euclidean inner product and componentwise derivatives.
The fixed point has t>0; restricting time to (t/2,3t/2) keeps a neighborhood inside the domain.

R001.justification: Expand v·v as the finite sum of squared real components. The scalar product rule follows by writing the product difference quotient as the sum of two factors' difference quotients, using differentiability and hence continuity. Apply it to each component square and add the finite sum. A locally constant scalar function has zero difference quotients. Thus the calculation used to obtain F001 is valid.

R001.fact: For a C² Euclidean-valued map v near a point and a time or spatial coordinate s, ∂_s²(v·v)=2|∂_s v|²+2v·∂_s²v. Consequently a locally unit-length v satisfies v·∂_s²v=−|∂_s v|².

grounds.reason: Joint smoothness provides two continuous coordinate derivatives.
The unit constraint holds on a neighborhood, rather than merely at the chosen point.
D002 identifies the norm square with the inner product and defines the coordinate second derivatives.
L1 places the point in the open positive-time domain.

R001.justification: Differentiate the finite-component identity ∂_s(v·v)=2Σ_k v_k∂_s v_k once more. The scalar product rule gives 2Σ_k[(∂_s v_k)²+v_k∂_s²v_k]. This is the asserted formula by the Euclidean norm definition. For v·v=1 its second derivative is zero; dividing the identity by 2 gives the stated consequence. It applies separately to time and each spatial coordinate, without requiring mixed-derivative commutation.

R002.fact: A compact C⊂ℝ^n is closed and bounded. There is R>0 with C⊂(−R,R)^n, also when C is empty; its complement is open.

grounds.reason: n is a finite positive integer.
F001 supplies a compact subset C of ℝ^n; S002 chooses it.

R002.justification: Euclidean space is Hausdorff, so its compact subsets are closed. The increasing cover by balls of positive integer radii has a finite subcover of C, giving a norm bound; each coordinate's absolute value is at most the Euclidean norm. Increase that bound strictly and take it positive to obtain R. For empty C any positive R works. These are routine compactness consequences at the point explicitly used in S002.

R002.fact: For a smooth u:ℝ^n×(0,∞)→ℝ^m, all its coordinate derivatives are smooth; finite sums, products and inner products of these derivatives are smooth. In particular e and e_t are smooth, with e_t=2u_t·u_tt+2Σ_{j=1}^n ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t. If u=q on the open set (ℝ^n\C)×int J, every positive-order mixed space/time derivative vanishes there. Each spatial function listed in F005 is continuous and has support contained in C for fixed r∈int J.

grounds.reason: Joint smoothness on the open positive-time domain is H002.
Coordinate derivatives and inner products are componentwise Euclidean operations.
e is the stated finite sum of derivative squares.
C is closed and u=q on the open exterior times int J, by F001.

R002.justification: Repeated differentiation preserves smoothness, and the finite product rule gives the displayed expression; smoothness allows interchange of the mixed derivatives. Locally u is constant on the stated open set, so its first derivatives vanish and iteration gives vanishing of every positive-order mixed derivative. The listed products and their differentiated products therefore vanish outside C at the indicated times. Smoothness implies continuity of each slice, and since C is closed, the closure of each nonzero set is still contained in C.

R002.fact: For finite n and R>0, Q=[−R,R]^n is compact and Lebesgue measurable, with measure (2R)^n<∞. If a real continuous f on ℝ^n vanishes outside a closed C⊂Q, then f is bounded on Q, measurable and absolutely integrable: for some finite M≥0, |f|≤M 1_Q and ∫|f|≤M(2R)^n.

grounds.reason: dx is standard Lebesgue measure, with the stated rectangle product normalization.
F002 gives positive finite R and C inside the open box.
S003 chooses R and Q and derives continuity and vanishing outside C for every listed slice.

R002.justification: Closed bounded intervals are compact and their finite product Q is compact; the product rectangle measure is the product of side lengths 2R. A continuous real function is Borel measurable, hence Lebesgue measurable. On compact Q continuity gives a finite absolute bound (a finite subcover of neighborhoods on which |f| is locally bounded suffices). Outside Q, f=0. The measurable function M1_Q has finite integral M|Q|; monotonicity of the nonnegative Lebesgue integral yields the displayed bound and absolute integrability. This applies separately to each indicated r and j; no common slice bound is required here.

R002.fact: With t0>0, η=t0/4 and Q=[−R,R]^n for R>0, K=Q×[t0−η,t0+η] is a nonempty compact subset of ℝ^n×(0,∞). If e_t is continuous on that domain, there exists B≥0 with |e_t|≤B on K.

grounds.reason: L1 is t0>0.
Q is the compact box with R>0, and e_t is smooth.
The endpoints are 3t0/4 and 5t0/4 and the entire interval lies in int J.

R002.justification: The closed time interval is nonempty and compact with positive endpoints. Q is nonempty because it contains zero, and finite products of compact sets are compact. Absolute value composed with continuous e_t is continuous. A finite subcover of local neighborhoods where its values are bounded gives a finite bound on K; increasing that bound to a nonnegative number gives B. The bound is simultaneous in x and r, as required.

R003.fact: For a jointly smooth u:ℝ^n×(0,∞)→ℝ^m, the density e=|u_t|²+Σ_j|∂_{x_j}u|² is smooth and has time derivative 2u_t·u_tt+2Σ_j∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t. Its fixed-space time sections and fixed-time spatial sections are smooth on their respective domains.

grounds.reason: H002 supplies joint smoothness on the open positive-time domain.
D002 specifies finite-dimensional component derivatives, norm squares and finite spatial sums.
D003 is exactly this density.

R003.justification: Write each squared Euclidean norm as the finite sum of component squares. The one-variable product rule differentiates each square to twice its component times its time derivative. Joint smoothness gives equality ∂_t∂_{x_j}u=∂_{x_j}∂_t u componentwise, and restriction of smooth functions preserves smoothness. These are local calculus facts, including empty finite sums.

R003.fact: The box Q=[−R,R]^n is Lebesgue measurable. With R>0, |Q|=(2R)^n<∞ and finite B≥0, w=B1_Q is measurable, integrable, and ∫|w| dx=B|Q|. Consequently the displayed domination is by an integrable real function.

grounds.reason: N002 supplies Q, its finite volume, R>0 and finite B≥0 jointly at t0.
D001 specifies Lebesgue measure, its coordinate-product convention and dimension-zero normalization.
S002 derives the bound on Q and vanishing outside Q from C⊂(−R,R)^n.

R003.justification: Each closed coordinate interval is Borel, so their finite product box is measurable. A constant multiple of the indicator of a measurable finite-measure set is a simple integrable function with absolute integral |B| times the set's measure; B≥0 gives |B|=B. In dimension zero Q is the measure-one singleton.

R003.fact: For each k under L2, V(k):ℝ^n→ℝ is continuous, Lebesgue almost everywhere strongly measurable and integrable; as k→∞ it converges at every x to e_t(x,t0).

grounds.reason: Smoothness gives continuous spatial sections and differentiable time sections of e.
N002 gives integrability of e at all positive times and the positive time window.
F002 also supplies integrable domination for every permitted increment.
L2 makes all h(k) nonzero, places t0+h(k) in the time window and gives h(k)→0.

R003.justification: For each k the quotient is a scalar multiple of the difference of two continuous spatial sections, hence continuous. A continuous real function is Borel and Lebesgue measurable and strongly measurable: truncating its values to [−l,l] and rounding on a mesh 2^(−l) gives finite-valued measurable approximants converging pointwise. Finite linear combinations of the two integrable sections are integrable. The definition of the time derivative gives convergence of these difference quotients along any nonzero h(k)→0.

R003.fact: Whenever 0<|h|<η, the Lebesgue integral of (e(·,t0+h)−e(·,t0))/h equals (E(t0+h)−E(t0))/h. At every positive time the displayed products in N003 and their scalar multiples and finite sums are integrable.

grounds.reason: N002 gives integrability of both e sections, e_t and every displayed dot product; its window guarantees positive times.
D004 identifies E with the actual finite integral of e.
S001 identifies the derivative formula componentwise.
The increment is nonzero by L2.

R003.justification: For integrable real functions f,g and finite scalars a,b, af+bg is integrable by |af+bg|≤|a||f|+|b||g| and its integral is a∫f+b∫g. Apply this with coefficients 1/h and −1/h, then to the finite sum with coefficients 2. No exchange of an infinite sum or unsupported integral is involved.

R003.fact: For η>0, if every sequence h_k with 0<|h_k|<η and h_k→0 has energy quotients converging to L=∫e_t(x,t0) dx, then the full punctured quotient limit as h→0 is L. Because [t0−η,t0+η]⊂(0,∞), this proves the derivative of E at t0.

grounds.reason: F004 supplies convergence for every sequence in this punctured window.
N002 supplies η>0 and the containment in int[t0/2,3t0/2], with t0>0.
S005 explicitly supplies the failure-of-limit contradiction construction.

R003.justification: If the limit failed, there would be ε>0 such that for each δ>0 there is h with 0<|h|<min(η,δ) and quotient error at least ε. Choose such h_k with δ=1/(k+1). The elementary Archimedean property gives h_k→0, while every quotient error is ≥ε, contradicting F004. The limit is finite by N002, and on the positive time neighborhood the difference-quotient definition of differentiability applies. This verifies the argument already present in S005.

R004.fact: For jointly smooth u at fixed t0>0 and 1≤j≤n, g(x)=u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0) is smooth and ∂_{x_j}g=(∂_{x_j}u_t)·∂_{x_j}u+u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u.

grounds.reason: Joint smoothness provides all component derivatives and their continuity at positive times.
Derivatives and the dot product have the componentwise Euclidean meanings.

R004.justification: Expand the dot product into its finite sum of component products and apply the scalar product rule to each. Smoothness is preserved by derivatives, products and finite sums, giving the displayed identity and continuity of the derivative.

R004.fact: If a compact C lies in (−R,R)^n with R>0, there is an open neighborhood of the boundary of Q=[−R,R]^n disjoint from C. A function vanishing outside C therefore vanishes near that boundary; all points with j-th coordinate ±R lie outside C, even if other coordinates lie outside Q.

grounds.reason: C is compact, C⊂(−R,R)^n, R>0, and positive-order derivatives vanish outside C at t0∈int J.
g is a product containing those vanishing derivatives.

R004.justification: For nonempty C, the continuous positive function x↦min_{1≤k≤n}(R−|x_k|) has a positive minimum on C. A collar narrower than this minimum misses C. For empty C any collar works. The endpoint assertion follows directly from strict coordinate inequalities on C and is valid for every remaining-coordinate vector.

R004.fact: A continuous real function on a compact interval is bounded, measurable and absolutely Lebesgue integrable there. For a<b its oriented interval integral equals the Lebesgue integral over [a,b]. Also a continuous scalar function on a compact coordinate box is integrable against the finite Lebesgue measure restricted to that box (or the corresponding finite product measure). Finite measures are s-finite; ℝ with its usual norm is a complete real normed vector space.

grounds.reason: g is smooth, so its coordinate derivative is continuous.
The inserted derivative is continuous and the interval has endpoints −R<R.
R is finite positive and Q has finite volume.
Coordinate measures are standard Lebesgue measures, with the dimension-zero singleton convention.

R004.justification: Continuity on a compact set gives a finite uniform bound and Borel measurability; the absolute integral is bounded by that bound times the finite measure. Closed and half-open intervals differ only by endpoints of zero Lebesgue measure, and positive orientation preserves sign. A finite measure is already one finite summand in an s-finite decomposition. Completeness here is the usual completeness of real numbers, which implies convergence of real Cauchy sequences in the absolute-value norm.

R004.fact: For n≥1 and 1≤j≤n, iota gives a measure-preserving bijection from Qrest×[−R,R], with the product of restricted coordinate Lebesgue measures, onto Q=[−R,R]^n with restricted Lebesgue measure. Consequently integrals of integrable scalar functions agree under this identification. For n=1 the first factor is the measure-one singleton.

grounds.reason: Lebesgue measures have the specified coordinate-product normalization, including dimension zero.
n≥1 and the fixed j is a valid coordinate.
iota inserts r at j and preserves the original order of all other coordinates.
The domains are the closed coordinate boxes Qrest and Q, with finite restricted measures.

R004.justification: iota is a continuous coordinate permutation with continuous inverse on these product spaces. The pushforward product measure and restricted box measure agree on coordinate rectangles because both assign the product of the same coordinate lengths. Both are finite measures; uniqueness from the generating rectangle algebra gives equality on Borel sets. Completion extends the equality to Lebesgue measurable sets. The corresponding integral identity follows first for indicators and simple functions and then for integrable functions. The singleton factor contributes the multiplicative factor one when n=1. This justifies the author's displayed coordinate identification, without replacing the FTC/Fubini route.

R004.fact: If a,b,d are real absolutely integrable functions on ℝ^n, d=a+b, and all vanish outside C⊂Q, then ∫_Q d=0 implies ∫_{ℝ^n}a=−∫_{ℝ^n}b. Interchanging the two vectors in the Euclidean dot product leaves a unchanged.

grounds.reason: F001 supplies the derivative identity, support in C and absolute integrability for d=∂_{x_j}g and its two summands.
The Fubini/FTC computation proves the box integral of d is zero.
The dot product is the standard finite-dimensional real Euclidean one.

R004.justification: Vanishing outside Q makes whole-space and restricted-box integrals equal. Linearity for integrable real functions gives 0=∫d=∫a+∫b, whence the displayed conclusion by real algebra. Symmetry follows termwise from commutativity of multiplication in the finite coordinate sum defining the real dot product.

R004.fact: For smooth g:ℝ^n→ℝ and the coordinate insertion iota defined in S002, r↦g(iota(y,r)) is smooth and has derivative ∂_{x_j}g(iota(y,r)) at every r∈ℝ for every fixed y∈ℝ^(n−1).

grounds.reason: F001 establishes global smoothness of g.
iota fixes all other coordinates and varies the j-th coordinate with slope one.
The dimension is positive and j is a valid coordinate.

R004.justification: The insertion map is affine. The chain rule computes its composition derivative by pairing the differential of g with the j-th coordinate vector, which is exactly ∂_{x_j}g. Iterating this fact preserves smoothness; no boundary exception occurs because the line function is defined on all of ℝ.

R005.fact: For a finite family of Lebesgue-integrable real functions g_k and real constants a_k, Σ_k a_k g_k is integrable and its integral is Σ_k a_k∫g_k. Pointwise equality preserves these integrals, and the integral of the identically zero function is zero. Here this applies to g_0(x)=u_t(x,t0)·u_tt(x,t0) and g_j(x)=u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(x,t0), as well as the derivative products in N003.

grounds.reason: At any positive t0, instantiate its local interval with base t0; t0 lies in int J, and all the displayed scalar products are absolutely integrable.
The energy-derivative identity and all its finite-sum integrands are integrable.
Both sides' integrands in each coordinate integration-by-parts identity are absolutely integrable.
The combined integrand u_t·(u_tt−Delta u) is zero at every spatial point.
Delta is a finite coordinate sum and the dot product is the Euclidean inner product.

R005.justification: Finite linear combinations remain absolutely integrable by the triangle inequality. Linearity of the Lebesgue integral follows by decomposing integrable functions into positive and negative parts, where all resulting integral values are finite; iterating gives finite-sum linearity. Euclidean bilinearity identifies the combined function with the displayed finite combination. Equality of functions gives equality of their integrals, and zero integrates to zero. Empty spatial sums when n=0 obey the same identities.

R005.fact: If E is differentiable at every r>0 with derivative zero and f:ℝ→ℝ equals E on (0,∞), then f has derivative zero and is continuous at every r>0. Consequently for 0<s<t it is continuous on [s,t] and has derivative zero at every point of (s,t).

grounds.reason: F001 states differentiability and derivative zero at every positive time, with no remaining local assumption.
L2 gives 0<s<t and hence all points of [s,t] are positive.
S002 explicitly constructs the real function equal to E on positive times and zero elsewhere; in a sufficiently small neighborhood of any positive point it agrees with E.

R005.justification: For r>0, the neighborhood (r−r/2,r+r/2) is contained in positive times. Thus f and E have identical difference quotients near r and the same derivative. Differentiability implies continuity: the difference f(r+h)−f(r) is h times a quotient tending to the finite derivative, and hence tends to zero. Pointwise continuity on a neighborhood of each point of [s,t] implies continuity restricted to that interval. This supplies precisely M004's continuity and derivative hypotheses without any behavior at zero.

source_steps.text: Fix arbitrary x∈ℝ^n and a real t, temporarily assuming L1: t>0. By H002 the component functions are smooth near (x,t). H004 gives u·u=1 in that neighborhood. Differentiating this identity in time by the componentwise product rule gives 2u·u_t=0, hence u·u_t=0. All quantities in this paragraph are evaluated at (x,t).
H005 at (x,t) provides a real a with u_tt−Delta u=a u; choose one. By F001 and symmetry of the inner product, u_t·(u_tt−Delta u)=a(u_t·u)=0. No derivative of a has been taken.

The same twice-differentiated unit constraint gives 0=∂_t²(u·u)=2|u_t|²+2u·u_tt, so u·u_tt=−|u_t|². For each spatial coordinate j from 1 through n, differentiating twice in that coordinate gives 0=2|∂_{x_j}u|²+2u·∂_{x_jx_j}u, so u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=−|∂_{x_j}u|². Dotting the chosen normality equation with u and using u·u=1 yields a=u·u_tt−Σ_j u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=Σ_j|∂_{x_j}u|²−|u_t|². This calculation uses only the equation for a, and therefore holds for every real scalar satisfying that equation at this point. Substitution gives u_tt−Delta u=(Σ_j|∂_{x_j}u|²−|u_t|²)u. Combine this with F001 and F002, discharge L1 to retain t>0 as the quantifier condition, and universally quantify x and t. This proves all the asserted pointwise identities and the explicit equation.

Fix real t0 and assume L1: t0>0. Put J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. Its endpoints satisfy 0<t0/2<3t0/2<∞, so H006 provides a compact spatial set for that entire interval. H001 gives finite positive integer dimensions throughout.

Choose such a C from F001. A compact subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space is bounded; enlarging a bound gives a positive real R such that C⊂(−R,R)^n. Compactness also makes C closed, hence (ℝ^n\C)×int J is open. On this open set u=q. By H002 and the local derivative of a constant, every positive-order spatial or time derivative of u vanishes there. Differentiating a constant here uses the fixed vector q and requires no condition on its norm.

Choose R as in F002 and put Q=[−R,R]^n. It is compact and has finite Lebesgue measure |Q|=(2R)^n. By smoothness H002, finite sums and products of the derivatives occurring in e, e_t, u_t·u_tt, ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t, u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u, u_t·∂_{x_j}u and ∂_{x_j}(u_t·∂_{x_j}u) are continuous, and e,e_t are jointly smooth. At every fixed r∈int J each listed spatial function vanishes outside C by F003, and is bounded on Q by continuity on a compact set. Continuous real functions on ℝ^n are measurable; a bound on Q and zero values outside Q dominate their absolute values by a finite constant times the indicator of Q. That indicator is integrable with integral (2R)^n, so each function is absolutely integrable. This applies to every spatial coordinate j with 1≤j≤n, and to every r∈int J.

Define η=t0/4>0. Then [t0−η,t0+η]=[3t0/4,5t0/4]⊂(t0/2,3t0/2)=int J. The continuous real function |e_t| on the compact nonempty set Q×[t0−η,t0+η] is bounded. Taking a nonnegative bound proves that there exists B≥0 with |e_t(x,r)|≤B for every x∈Q and every r in this closed time interval.

Choose B from F004. The witnesses C,R,η,B and defined J,Q have all the asserted common-support, measure, regularity, integrability and bound properties by F001,F002,F003,F005,F004. In particular t0∈int J and e(·,t0) is integrable. Introduce the existential quantifiers over C,R,η,B before closing their scope; discharge L1 and universally quantify the arbitrary t0. This proves the detailed common-support assertion and, by the arbitrariness of the positive base time, integrability of e(·,t) for every t>0.

Fix real t0 and temporarily assume L1: t0>0. Instantiate N002 to choose jointly C,R,η,B, and set J=[t0/2,3t0/2], Q=[−R,R]^n as in that statement. In particular the indicated time window lies in int J. By H002 the product rule and equality of mixed coordinate derivatives give, at every (x,t) with t>0,
e_t(x,t)=2u_t(x,t)·u_tt(x,t)+2Σ_{j=1}^n ∂_{x_j}u(x,t)·∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t).
N002 makes every term on the right integrable at each such time.

For each fixed spatial point x∈Q and each real nonzero increment h0 with |h0|<η, apply M004 to the real function of time r↦e(x,r), extended by zero on nonpositive times, and its derivative r↦e_t(x,r) on positive times (also assigned zero elsewhere). Use the ordered endpoints min(t0,t0+h0), max(t0,t0+h0). Their closed interval lies inside [t0−η,t0+η]⊂int J, where smoothness gives continuity and the stated derivative. M004 gives an intermediate derivative equal to the secant slope. For either sign of h0 that slope is (e(x,t0+h0)−e(x,t0))/h0. The uniform bound in N002 therefore gives its absolute value at most B. Outside Q both densities are zero by N002. Thus throughout ℝ^n,
|(e(x,t0+h0)−e(x,t0))/h0|≤B 1_Q(x).
The right side is integrable, since Q has finite measure and B is finite and nonnegative.

Take an arbitrary real sequence h and temporarily assume L2: for every natural k, 0<|h(k)|<η, and h(k)→0. Define V(k)(x)=(e(x,t0+h(k))−e(x,t0))/h(k) and w(x)=B 1_Q(x). Each V(k) is a continuous real function of x, hence strongly measurable and in particular almost everywhere strongly measurable for Lebesgue measure; it is integrable either by N002 and linearity or by F002. By F002, |V(k)(x)|≤w(x) everywhere, and w is integrable. By the pointwise time differentiability supplied by smoothness, V(k)(x)→e_t(x,t0) for every x. All these facts concern the real codomain and the Lebesgue measure on ℝ^n.

Apply M001 with its measure space ℝ^n with Lebesgue measure, codomain ℝ, sequence V, limit x↦e_t(x,t0), and bound w. The four analytic premises were proved in F003, and ℝ has the required real normed-space structure. It follows that ∫ V(k)(x) dx→∫ e_t(x,t0) dx. N002 and D004 identify, by linearity of finite integrals, ∫ V(k)(x) dx=(E(t0+h(k))−E(t0))/h(k). Discharge L2 and quantify the arbitrary sequence h: every sequence of nonzero increments in this punctured η-window tending to zero gives energy quotients tending to ∫ e_t(x,t0) dx.

F004 implies the full punctured limit as the real increment tends to zero. Indeed failure of that limit would give some fixed positive error and arbitrarily small nonzero increments within the η-window whose quotient errors are at least that amount. Choosing one at distance less than 1/(k+1) for each natural k would form a sequence contradicting F004. This is the sequential criterion for limits in ℝ, with the entire window inside positive time. Thus the actual finite integral E is differentiable at t0 and
E'(t0)=∫_{ℝ^n}e_t(x,t0) dx.
Combine this with F001 and the integrability exported in N002. Discharge L1 and universally quantify t0; no choices C,R,η,B enter the conclusion. This proves the claimed derivative formula and integrability.

Fix real t0 and assume L1: t0>0, and fix any spatial coordinate j with 1≤j≤n (H001). Choose C,R from N002 at this time and set Q=[−R,R]^n. Put g(x)=u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0). It is smooth by H002. Since C is compact and contained in the open box (−R,R)^n, it has positive distance from the boundary of Q; N002 therefore makes g zero on a neighborhood of that boundary. The product rule gives
∂_{x_j}g(x)=∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0)+u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(x,t0).
N002 says the derivative and each summand are continuous, supported in C, and integrable on ℝ^n and hence on Q.

Let iota(y,r) insert the real r in coordinate j, with y∈ℝ^(n−1) giving all remaining coordinates in their original order, and put phi(y)(r)=g(iota(y,r)). For each y, phi(y) is smooth on ℝ with derivative r↦∂_{x_j}g(iota(y,r)). Its endpoint values at −R and R are zero, since those points have a coordinate on the boundary of Q and in any event lie outside C. Apply M003 with real codomain, endpoints −R,R, function phi(y), and the displayed derivative. The derivative exists at every point of [−R,R] and is continuous, hence interval integrable there. We obtain
∫_{−R}^{R} ∂_{x_j}g(iota(y,r)) dr=phi(y)(R)−phi(y)(−R)=0.
This holds for every y∈ℝ^(n−1). The oriented integral agrees with the Lebesgue integral on the closed interval here, since −R<R and the endpoints have measure zero.

Set Qrest=[−R,R]^(n−1). Under iota, Qrest×[−R,R] is exactly Q with its coordinates reordered. Standard Lebesgue measure is the product of the coordinate measures (D001); reordering these factors preserves the measure, since on any coordinate rectangle both descriptions give the product of the same side lengths. Thus the integral on Q is the product-measure integral of (y,r)↦∂_{x_j}g(iota(y,r)) with Lebesgue measures restricted to Qrest and [−R,R]. This scalar function is continuous on a compact box and bounded there, hence integrable for that finite product measure. M002 now gives
∫_Q ∂_{x_j}g dx=∫_{Qrest}(∫_{[−R,R]}∂_{x_j}g(iota(y,r)) dr) dy=0
by F002. When n=1, Qrest is the singleton ℝ^0 of measure one, so this formula reduces to the very same one-variable identity. Outside Q all terms in F001 vanish. Integrating F001 over ℝ^n, using the finiteness of both summand integrals and symmetry of the dot product, yields
∫_{ℝ^n}∂_{x_j}u(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t0) dx=−∫_{ℝ^n}u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(x,t0) dx.
Quantify the arbitrary coordinate j, discharge L1, and quantify t0. This proves the claimed integration-by-parts identity including absolute integrability.

Fix real t0 and assume L1: t0>0. H002 makes all derivative notation classical. N002 proves e(·,t0) and all derivative products below are integrable, so E is the finite energy integral in D004. N003 proves differentiability and its integral formula. Substitute that formula and use N004 for each coordinate, then use finite-sum linearity and the definition of Delta:
E'(t0)=2∫_{ℝ^n}u_t(x,t0)·u_tt(x,t0) dx+2Σ_{j=1}^n∫_{ℝ^n}∂_{x_j}u(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t0) dx
=2∫_{ℝ^n}u_t(x,t0)·u_tt(x,t0) dx−2Σ_{j=1}^n∫_{ℝ^n}u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(x,t0) dx
=2∫_{ℝ^n}u_t(x,t0)·(u_tt(x,t0)−Delta u(x,t0)) dx=0.
The last equality is N001 pointwise. Every passage uses finite integrals from N002, with no boundary term left over. Discharge L1 and universally quantify t0. Hence E is differentiable everywhere on (0,∞) with E'=0 there.

Fix arbitrary real s,t and assume L2: 0<s<t. Apply M004 to the real function equal to E on positive times and zero elsewhere, with derivative function zero, and endpoints s,t. By F001, E is differentiable at every point of [s,t], so it is continuous there and has derivative zero on (s,t). M004 gives an interior point whose derivative zero equals (E(t)−E(s))/(t−s). Since t−s>0, E(t)=E(s). Discharge L2 and quantify s,t. Any pair of positive times is either equal or can be ordered in this way, so symmetry of equality gives constancy on (0,∞). Together with N002 and F001 this proves P. The density is exactly |u_t|²+Σ_j|∂_{x_j}u|² from D003, so no factor 1/2 is introduced and no assertion at time zero is used.

roots.statement: n≥1 and m≥1 are integer dimensions.
u:ℝ^n×(0,∞)→ℝ^m is jointly smooth.
q∈ℝ^m is fixed and |q|=1.
For every x∈ℝ^n and t>0, |u(x,t)|=1.
For every x∈ℝ^n and t>0 there exists a real scalar a such that u_tt(x,t)−Delta u(x,t)=a u(x,t). No regularity of any selected scalar is assumed.
For every pair of real times 0<s<t<∞ there exists a compact set C_[s,t]⊂ℝ^n such that u(x,r)=q whenever x∉C_[s,t] and r∈[s,t].

Let A be any measurable space with measure μ and G any normed additive commutative group with a real normed vector-space structure. For F:ℕ→A→G, f:A→G and bound:A→ℝ, if each F(k) is μ-almost everywhere strongly measurable, bound is μ-integrable, ||F(k)(z)||≤bound(z) for μ-almost every z for every k, and F(k)(z)→f(z) as k→∞ for μ-almost every z, then ∫ F(k) dμ→∫ f dμ.

hypotheses: A is a measurable space, μ a measure, and G is a normed additive commutative group and real normed space.
Every F(k) is μ-almost everywhere strongly measurable.
bound is μ-integrable.
For each k, ||F(k)(z)||≤bound(z) for μ-almost every z.
For μ-almost every z, F(k)(z) tends to f(z).

result.value: Use one ambient Euclidean representation throughout: Space d = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d) = PiLp 2 (fun _ => ℝ). Its norm and real inner product are the Euclidean ones; PiLp.inner_apply identifies the latter with the coordinate dot product. Fin n labels the original n coordinates by j.val + 1; it introduces neither a missing endpoint nor an extra coordinate. PiLp.single 2 j 1 is the unit vector in coordinate j, so spatial is the Fréchet derivative evaluated on that vector. ut and utt are successive ordinary time derivatives, uxx successive same-coordinate spatial derivatives, and utx is the spatial derivative of ut. Under H002 equality of mixed derivatives identifies utx with the time derivative of ux; proving this identification is part of T004/T007, not a hidden assumption. densityTime is the ACTUAL time derivative of the density, not an assumed product formula. The parameter u is an arbitrary total ambient representative; H002 and all geometric hypotheses concern only positive times. Any source map extends by zero for t≤0, without requiring boundary regularity, and restriction recovers it. Since positive times form an open set, derivatives of all orders and energy germs there depend only on that restriction. No conclusion concerns the chosen exterior values. ContDiffOn uses (∞ : ℕ∞ω), meaning every finite derivative order, not ω (analyticity) or the top element of ℕ∞ω. Header definitions assert no regularity or integrability. The total Bochner integral in energy gains its intended finite Lebesgue meaning only after T003 proves integrability. volume is standard normalized Euclidean Lebesgue measure; EuclideanSpace.volume_preserving_symm_measurableEquiv_toLp identifies it with product coordinate Lebesgue measure. In N002, iteratedFDeriv of positive natural order is the multilinear encoding of all mixed space/time derivatives: evaluation on coordinate unit vectors recovers them, and multilinearity plus the coordinate basis gives the converse. All this is in the same Euclidean representation; local product-coordinate measure transport in T008 is checked inside that obligation. No M ports are retained: the four supplied library theorems are used directly under their actual hypotheses. H003 is preserved although the source proof never needs the norm of q. For measures, ENNReal.ofReal ((2*R)^n) encodes a nonnegative real box volume; R>0 and the explicit non-top clause prevent treating an infinite mass as a real finite integral. Integrable means almost everywhere strong measurability together with finite integral of the norm. The supplied dominated-convergence theorem requires these norm and measurability conditions, not merely pointwise convergence. For the scalar FTC, ℝ supplies completeness; the derivative must exist on the unordered closed interval and its function must be interval integrable. Fubini will be used with finite restricted coordinate measures, hence s-finite, and a genuinely integrable real function. These typeclass capabilities are properties of the chosen standard spaces and measures, not additional hypotheses on the wave map.

value.statement: For every t>0, e(·,t) is Lebesgue integrable on ℝ^n. More precisely, for every t0>0 there exist a compact C⊂ℝ^n and real R>0, η>0 and B≥0 with the following properties. Set J=[t0/2,3t0/2] and Q=[−R,R]^n. Then C⊂(−R,R)^n, |Q|=(2R)^n<∞, [t0−η,t0+η]⊂int J, and u(x,r)=q for x∉C,r∈J. All positive-order space/time derivatives of u vanish on (ℝ^n\C)×int J. argument.text: Fix arbitrary x∈ℝ^n and a real t, temporarily assuming L1: t>0. By H002 the component functions are smooth near (x,t). H004 gives u·u=1 in that neighborhood. Differentiating this identity in time by the componentwise product rule gives 2u·u_t=0, hence u·u_t=0. All quantities in this paragraph are evaluated at (x,t).
H005 at (x,t) provides a real a with u_tt−Delta u=a u; choose one. By F001 and symmetry of the inner product, u_t·(u_tt−Delta u)=a(u_t·u)=0. No derivative of a has been taken.

The same twice-differentiated unit constraint gives 0=∂_t²(u·u)=2|u_t|²+2u·u_tt, so u·u_tt=−|u_t|². For each spatial coordinate j from 1 through n, differentiating twice in that coordinate gives 0=2|∂_{x_j}u|²+2u·∂_{x_jx_j}u, so u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=−|∂_{x_j}u|². Dotting the chosen normality equation with u and using u·u=1 yields a=u·u_tt−Σ_j u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=Σ_j|∂_{x_j}u|²−|u_t|². This calculation uses only the equation for a, and therefore holds for every real scalar satisfying that equation at this point. Substitution gives u_tt−Delta u=(Σ_j|∂_{x_j}u|²−|u_t|²)u. Combine this with F001 and F002, discharge L1 to retain t>0 as the quantifier condition, and universally quantify x and t. This proves all the asserted pointwise identities and the explicit equation.

argument.text: Fix real t0 and assume L1: t0>0. Put J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. Its endpoints satisfy 0<t0/2<3t0/2<∞, so H006 provides a compact spatial set for that entire interval. H001 gives finite positive integer dimensions throughout.

argument.text: Choose such a C from F001. A compact subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space is bounded; enlarging a bound gives a positive real R such that C⊂(−R,R)^n. Compactness also makes C closed, hence (ℝ^n\C)×int J is open. On this open set u=q. By H002 and the local derivative of a constant, every positive-order spatial or time derivative of u vanishes there. Differentiating a constant here uses the fixed vector q and requires no condition on its norm.

produces.statement: All positive-order space/time derivatives of u vanish on (ℝ^n\C)×int J.

argument.text: Choose R as in F002 and put Q=[−R,R]^n. It is compact and has finite Lebesgue measure |Q|=(2R)^n. By smoothness H002, finite sums and products of the derivatives occurring in e, e_t, u_t·u_tt, ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t, u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u, u_t·∂_{x_j}u and ∂_{x_j}(u_t·∂_{x_j}u) are continuous, and e,e_t are jointly smooth. At every fixed r∈int J each listed spatial function vanishes outside C by F003, and is bounded on Q by continuity on a compact set. Continuous real functions on ℝ^n are measurable; a bound on Q and zero values outside Q dominate their absolute values by a finite constant times the indicator of Q. That indicator is integrable with integral (2R)^n, so each function is absolutely integrable. This applies to every spatial coordinate j with 1≤j≤n, and to every r∈int J.

produces.statement: Q has measure (2R)^n<∞. The functions e,e_t are smooth. For every r∈int J and 1≤j≤n, the spatial functions e(·,r), e_t(·,r), u_t·u_tt, ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t, u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u, u_t·∂_{x_j}u, and ∂_{x_j}(u_t·∂_{x_j}u), evaluated at r, are continuous, supported in C, measurable, bounded on Q and absolutely integrable.

argument.text: Define η=t0/4>0. Then [t0−η,t0+η]=[3t0/4,5t0/4]⊂(t0/2,3t0/2)=int J. The continuous real function |e_t| on the compact nonempty set Q×[t0−η,t0+η] is bounded. Taking a nonnegative bound proves that there exists B≥0 with |e_t(x,r)|≤B for every x∈Q and every r in this closed time interval.

produces.statement: There exists B≥0 with |e_t(x,r)|≤B for all x∈Q, r∈[t0−η,t0+η], and η>0 with this interval contained in int J.

argument.text: Choose B from F004. The witnesses C,R,η,B and defined J,Q have all the asserted common-support, measure, regularity, integrability and bound properties by F001,F002,F003,F005,F004. In particular t0∈int J and e(·,t0) is integrable. Introduce the existential quantifiers over C,R,η,B before closing their scope; discharge L1 and universally quantify the arbitrary t0. This proves the detailed common-support assertion and, by the arbitrariness of the positive base time, integrability of e(·,t) for every t>0.

argument.text:
Fix real t0 and temporarily assume L1: t0>0. Instantiate N002 to choose jointly C,R,η,B, and set J=[t0/2,3t0/2], Q=[−R,R]^n as in that statement. In particular the indicated time window lies in int J. By H002 the product rule and equality of mixed coordinate derivatives give, at every (x,t) with t>0,
e_t(x,t)=2u_t(x,t)·u_tt(x,t)+2Σ_{j=1}^n ∂_{x_j}u(x,t)·∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t).
N002 makes every term on the right integrable at each such time.

produces.statement: For all x∈ℝ^n and t>0, e_t(x,t)=2u_t(x,t)·u_tt(x,t)+2Σ_{j=1}^n∂_{x_j}u(x,t)·∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t); all summands as spatial functions at each positive time are integrable.

argument.text:
For each fixed spatial point x∈Q and each real nonzero increment h0 with |h0|<η, apply M004 to the real function of time r↦e(x,r), extended by zero on nonpositive times, and its derivative r↦e_t(x,r) on positive times (also assigned zero elsewhere). Use the ordered endpoints min(t0,t0+h0), max(t0,t0+h0). Their closed interval lies inside [t0−η,t0+η]⊂int J, where smoothness gives continuity and the stated derivative. M004 gives an intermediate derivative equal to the secant slope. For either sign of h0 that slope is (e(x,t0+h0)−e(x,t0))/h0. The uniform bound in N002 therefore gives its absolute value at most B. Outside Q both densities are zero by N002. Thus throughout ℝ^n,
|(e(x,t0+h0)−e(x,t0))/h0|≤B 1_Q(x).
The right side is integrable, since Q has finite measure and B is finite and nonnegative.

produces.statement: For all x∈ℝ^n and all real h0 with 0<|h0|<η, |(e(x,t0+h0)−e(x,t0))/h0|≤B 1_Q(x). The function B 1_Q is Lebesgue integrable.

argument.text: Take an arbitrary real sequence h and temporarily assume L2: for every natural k, 0<|h(k)|<η, and h(k)→0. Define V(k)(x)=(e(x,t0+h(k))−e(x,t0))/h(k) and w(x)=B 1_Q(x). Each V(k) is a continuous real function of x, hence strongly measurable and in particular almost everywhere strongly measurable for Lebesgue measure; it is integrable either by N002 and linearity or by F002. By F002, |V(k)(x)|≤w(x) everywhere, and w is integrable. By the pointwise time differentiability supplied by smoothness, V(k)(x)→e_t(x,t0) for every x. All these facts concern the real codomain and the Lebesgue measure on ℝ^n.

produces.statement: Each V(k) is almost everywhere strongly measurable for dx, w is integrable, |V(k)(x)|≤w(x) for every k and x, and V(k)(x)→e_t(x,t0) for every x.

argument.text: Apply M001 with its measure space ℝ^n with Lebesgue measure, codomain ℝ, sequence V, limit x↦e_t(x,t0), and bound w. The four analytic premises were proved in F003, and ℝ has the required real normed-space structure. It follows that ∫ V(k)(x) dx→∫ e_t(x,t0) dx. N002 and D004 identify, by linearity of finite integrals, ∫ V(k)(x) dx=(E(t0+h(k))−E(t0))/h(k). Discharge L2 and quantify the arbitrary sequence h: every sequence of nonzero increments in this punctured η-window tending to zero gives energy quotients tending to ∫ e_t(x,t0) dx.

produces.statement: For every sequence zeta:ℕ→ℝ, if 0<|zeta(k)|<η for every k and zeta(k)→0, then (E(t0+zeta(k))−E(t0))/zeta(k)→∫_{ℝ^n}e_t(x,t0) dx.

argument.text:
F004 implies the full punctured limit as the real increment tends to zero. Indeed failure of that limit would give some fixed positive error and arbitrarily small nonzero increments within the η-window whose quotient errors are at least that amount. Choosing one at distance less than 1/(k+1) for each natural k would form a sequence contradicting F004. This is the sequential criterion for limits in ℝ, with the entire window inside positive time. Thus the actual finite integral E is differentiable at t0 and
E'(t0)=∫_{ℝ^n}e_t(x,t0) dx.
Combine this with F001 and the integrability exported in N002. Discharge L1 and universally quantify t0; no choices C,R,η,B enter the conclusion. This proves the claimed derivative formula and integrability.

applications.bindings: For each x∈Q and nonzero h0 with |h0|<η, take f(r)=e(x,r) and f'(r)=e_t(x,r) on positive r, extend both by zero elsewhere, and take a=min(t0,t0+h0), b=max(t0,t0+h0).
hypothesis_checks: H002 and N002 give smoothness and hence continuity on this closed interval, contained in the positive time window.
The time derivative on that interval is e_t by H002 and F001; no extension point at r≤0 lies in the interval.

applications.bindings: Set A=ℝ^n with its Lebesgue measurable space and μ=dx, G=ℝ, source F(k)=V(k), source f(x)=e_t(x,t0), and source bound=w=B 1_Q.
hypothesis_checks: The Euclidean Lebesgue space is a measurable space with measure dx; ℝ is a normed additive commutative group and real normed space.
F003 gives almost everywhere strong measurability of each V(k), from its continuity.
F003 and F002 give integrability of w, since it is B times the indicator of the finite-measure box Q.
F003 gives the pointwise bound |V(k)(x)|≤w(x), which implies the required almost everywhere bounds.
F003 gives convergence to e_t(x,t0) at every x from time differentiability, hence almost everywhere.

iota(y,r) inserts r as the j-th coordinate and the coordinates of y in their original order as the remaining coordinates.

locals.type: family of real functions indexed by ℝ^(n−1)
locals.declaration: Define phi(y)(r)=g(iota(y,r)).
Set Qrest=[−R,R]^(n−1), with the singleton convention in dimension zero.

argument.text:
Fix real t0 and assume L1: t0>0, and fix any spatial coordinate j with 1≤j≤n (H001). Choose C,R from N002 at this time and set Q=[−R,R]^n. Put g(x)=u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0). It is smooth by H002. Since C is compact and contained in the open box (−R,R)^n, it has positive distance from the boundary of Q; N002 therefore makes g zero on a neighborhood of that boundary. The product rule gives
∂_{x_j}g(x)=∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0)+u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(x,t0).
N002 says the derivative and each summand are continuous, supported in C, and integrable on ℝ^n and hence on Q.

produces.statement: g is smooth and zero near the boundary of Q. Its derivative ∂_{x_j}g=∂_{x_j}u_t(·,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(·,t0)+u_t(·,t0)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(·,t0); the derivative and both summands are supported in C and absolutely integrable.

argument.text:
Let iota(y,r) insert the real r in coordinate j, with y∈ℝ^(n−1) giving all remaining coordinates in their original order, and put phi(y)(r)=g(iota(y,r)). For each y, phi(y) is smooth on ℝ with derivative r↦∂_{x_j}g(iota(y,r)). Its endpoint values at −R and R are zero, since those points have a coordinate on the boundary of Q and in any event lie outside C. Apply M003 with real codomain, endpoints −R,R, function phi(y), and the displayed derivative. The derivative exists at every point of [−R,R] and is continuous, hence interval integrable there. We obtain
∫_{−R}^{R} ∂_{x_j}g(iota(y,r)) dr=phi(y)(R)−phi(y)(−R)=0.
This holds for every y∈ℝ^(n−1). The oriented integral agrees with the Lebesgue integral on the closed interval here, since −R<R and the endpoints have measure zero.

Set Qrest=[−R,R]^(n−1). Under iota, Qrest×[−R,R] is exactly Q with its coordinates reordered. Standard Lebesgue measure is the product of the coordinate measures (D001); reordering these factors preserves the measure, since on any coordinate rectangle both descriptions give the product of the same side lengths. Thus the integral on Q is the product-measure integral of (y,r)↦∂_{x_j}g(iota(y,r)) with Lebesgue measures restricted to Qrest and [−R,R]. This scalar function is continuous on a compact box and bounded there, hence integrable for that finite product measure. M002 now gives
∫_Q ∂_{x_j}g dx=∫_{Qrest}(∫_{[−R,R]}∂_{x_j}g(iota(y,r)) dr) dy=0
by F002. When n=1, Qrest is the singleton ℝ^0 of measure one, so this formula reduces to the very same one-variable identity. Outside Q all terms in F001 vanish. Integrating F001 over ℝ^n, using the finiteness of both summand integrals and symmetry of the dot product, yields
∫_{ℝ^n}∂_{x_j}u(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t0) dx=−∫_{ℝ^n}u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(x,t0) dx.
Quantify the arbitrary coordinate j, discharge L1, and quantify t0. This proves the claimed integration-by-parts identity including absolute integrability.

applications.bindings: For every fixed remaining-coordinate vector y, take V=ℝ, a=−R, b=R, f=phi(y), and f'(r)=∂_{x_j}g(iota(y,r)).
hypothesis_checks: ℝ is a complete normed additive commutative group and real normed space.
F001 gives global smoothness of g; coordinate insertion is affine, so the stated derivative of phi(y) exists on all of [−R,R], including endpoints.
The derivative is continuous on the compact interval, and therefore Lebesgue interval integrable.

applications.bindings: Take A=ℝ^(n−1), B=ℝ, μ=Lebesgue measure restricted to Qrest, ν=Lebesgue measure restricted to [−R,R], V=ℝ, and f(y,r)=∂_{x_j}g(iota(y,r)). Use the coordinate-product identification of Q explained in S003.
hypothesis_checks: The Borel/Lebesgue measurable coordinate spaces carry the stated measures; their restrictions to these boxes are finite and hence s-finite, also for n=1 with the measure-one singleton factor.
The scalar codomain ℝ has the required normed additive commutative group and real normed-space structures.
F001 gives continuity of the derivative; composed with iota it is bounded and measurable on this finite-measure compact product box, which proves product integrability before applying M002.

Fix any real s.

argument.text:
Fix real t0 and assume L1: t0>0. H002 makes all derivative notation classical. N002 proves e(·,t0) and all derivative products below are integrable, so E is the finite energy integral in D004. N003 proves differentiability and its integral formula. Substitute that formula and use N004 for each coordinate, then use finite-sum linearity and the definition of Delta:
E'(t0)=2∫_{ℝ^n}u_t(x,t0)·u_tt(x,t0) dx+2Σ_{j=1}^n∫_{ℝ^n}∂_{x_j}u(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t0) dx
=2∫_{ℝ^n}u_t(x,t0)·u_tt(x,t0) dx−2Σ_{j=1}^n∫_{ℝ^n}u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(x,t0) dx
=2∫_{ℝ^n}u_t(x,t0)·(u_tt(x,t0)−Delta u(x,t0)) dx=0.
The last equality is N001 pointwise. Every passage uses finite integrals from N002, with no boundary term left over. Discharge L1 and universally quantify t0. Hence E is differentiable everywhere on (0,∞) with E'=0 there.

produces.statement: For every tau>0, E is differentiable at tau and E'(tau)=0.

argument.text: Fix arbitrary real s,t and assume L2: 0<s<t. Apply M004 to the real function equal to E on positive times and zero elsewhere, with derivative function zero, and endpoints s,t. By F001, E is differentiable at every point of [s,t], so it is continuous there and has derivative zero on (s,t). M004 gives an interior point whose derivative zero equals (E(t)−E(s))/(t−s). Since t−s>0, E(t)=E(s). Discharge L2 and quantify s,t. Any pair of positive times is either equal or can be ordered in this way, so symmetry of equality gives constancy on (0,∞). Together with N002 and F001 this proves P. The density is exactly |u_t|²+Σ_j|∂_{x_j}u|² from D003, so no factor 1/2 is introduced and no assertion at time zero is used.

applications.bindings: Take f(r)=E(r) for r>0 and f(r)=0 for r≤0; take f'(r)=0 for all real r; set a=s and b=t.
hypothesis_checks: F001 gives differentiability at each point of [s,t]⊂(0,∞), hence continuity there; the extension equals E throughout a neighborhood of that interval.
F001 gives derivative zero at every point of (s,t), as required for the chosen f'.

result.text:
1: # Conservation of energy for a sphere-valued wave map
2: 
3: ## Original exercise
4: 
5: Lawrence C. Evans, *Partial Differential Equations*, second edition,
6: Graduate Studies in Mathematics 19, AMS, 2010, section 12.6, exercise 14,
7: printed page 694. The preceding exercise 13 defines the sphere-valued
8: wave map. ISBN: 978-0-8218-4974-3.
9: 
10: > 14. Prove that if \(\mathbf u\) is a wave map into the unit sphere,
11: > with compact support in space, we have conservation of energy:
12: > \[
13: > \frac{d}{dt}\int_{\mathbb R^n}
14: >       |\mathbf u_t|^2+|D\mathbf u|^2\,dx=0.
15: > \]
16: 
17: ## Fixed interpretation and complete target
18: 
19: A sphere-valued map cannot vanish outside a compact set. As approved by
20: the user on 2026-10-23, interpret spatial compact support as compact support
21: of a perturbation from a **fixed unit vector**, locally uniformly in time.
22: This is a disclosed nontrivial interpretation, not a claimed author-issued
23: correction.
24: 
25: Let \(n,m\geq1\) be integers and let
26: \(u:\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^m\) be jointly smooth.
27: Fix \(q\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(|q|=1\). Assume:
28: 
29: 1. \(|u(x,t)|=1\) for all \(x\) and \(t>0\).
30: 2. The acceleration \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu\) is normal to the sphere at
31:    \(u\): at each point there is a real scalar \(a(x,t)\) with
32:    \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu=a u\). No regularity of the selected scalar is
33:    assumed.
34: 3. For every \(0<s<t<\infty\), a compact set
35:    \(C_{[s,t]}\subset\mathbb R^n\) exists such that \(u(x,r)=q\) for
36:    \(x\notin C_{[s,t]}\), \(r\in[s,t]\).
37: 
38: With Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure, define
39: 
40: \[
41: e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+\sum_{j=1}^n|\partial_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2,
42: \qquad E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e(x,t)\,dx.
43: \]
44: 
45: The spatial gradient square is the Frobenius square, and
46: \(\Delta_xu=\sum_j\partial_{x_jx_j}u\) component by component.
47: Prove integrability of \(e(\cdot,t)\), differentiability of \(E\),
48: and \(E'(t)=0\) for every \(t>0\). No assertion at time zero is required.
49: 
50: ## Fixed natural-language proof
51: 
52: ### 1. Tangency and the wave-map equation
53: 
54: Differentiate \(u\cdot u=1\) in time. The product rule gives
55: \(2u\cdot u_t=0\), so
56: 
57: \[
58: u\cdot u_t=0,\qquad
59: u_t\cdot(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu)=a(u_t\cdot u)=0.          \tag{1}
60: \]
61: 
62: No derivative of \(a\) is needed. The familiar explicit equation also
63: follows from the assumptions: twice differentiating the unit constraint
64: gives \(u\cdot u_{tt}=-|u_t|^2\) and
65: \(u\cdot\partial_{x_jx_j}u=-|\partial_{x_j}u|^2\).
66: Dotting the normality equation with \(u\), using \(|u|^2=1\), yields
67: \(a=\sum_j|\partial_{x_j}u|^2-|u_t|^2\). This is a consequence,
68: not an additional PDE assumption.
69: 
70: ### 2. Common compact support and integrability
71: 
72: Fix \(t_0>0\), put \(J=[t_0/2,3t_0/2]\), and choose its compact
73: spatial set \(C\) from assumption 3. Since \(C\) is bounded, choose
74: \(R>0\) with \(C\subset(-R,R)^n\) and set \(Q=[-R,R]^n\).
75: The box has finite Lebesgue measure \((2R)^n\).
76: 
77: On the open set \((\mathbb R^n\setminus C)\times\operatorname{int}J\),
78: the map equals the constant \(q\), so all its positive-order
79: derivatives vanish. At interior times, \(e\), \(e_t\), and the
80: derivative products used below consequently vanish outside \(C\).
81: They are continuous by smoothness; their spatial sections are measurable,
82: bounded on \(Q\), and supported there. Their absolute integrals are
83: bounded by a finite constant times \(|Q|\). This proves integrability
84: of \(e(\cdot,t_0)\) and of all later terms. Since \(t_0\) was arbitrary,
85: the energy is a finite, well-defined integral at every positive time.
86: 
87: ### 3. Differentiate the energy integral
88: 
89: The product rule and equality of mixed derivatives give
90: 
91: \[
92: e_t=2u_t\cdot u_{tt}
93:    +2\sum_{j=1}^n\partial_{x_j}u\cdot\partial_{x_j}u_t.           \tag{2}
94: \]
95: 
96: Choose \(\eta>0\) so that
97: \([t_0-\eta,t_0+\eta]\subset\operatorname{int}J\).
98: Continuity of (2) on the compact box
99: \(Q\times[t_0-\eta,t_0+\eta]\) gives a finite bound \(|e_t|\leq B\).
100: For \(0<|h|<\eta\), the one-variable mean value theorem at fixed
101: \(x\) therefore gives
102: 
103: \[
104: \left|\frac{e(x,t_0+h)-e(x,t_0)}h\right|
105: \leq B\mathbf1_Q(x).
106: \]
107: 
108: Outside \(Q\), both densities vanish, so the bound holds throughout
109: \(\mathbb R^n\). The right side is integrable. The difference
110: quotients converge pointwise to \(e_t(x,t_0)\). Dominated convergence
111: and linearity for these integrable functions now prove
112: 
113: \[
114: E'(t_0)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e_t(x,t_0)\,dx.            \tag{3}
115: \]
116: 
117: This establishes differentiability of the actual finite integral.
118: 
119: ### 4. Integration by parts and cancellation
120: 
121: For each spatial index \(j\), at time \(t_0\) put
122: \(g_j(x)=u_t(x,t_0)\cdot\partial_{x_j}u(x,t_0)\).
123: It is smooth and vanishes on a neighborhood of the boundary of \(Q\),
124: because \(C\subset\operatorname{int}Q\). The product rule gives
125: 
126: \[
127: \partial_{x_j}g_j
128: =\partial_{x_j}u_t\cdot\partial_{x_j}u
129:  +u_t\cdot\partial_{x_jx_j}u.
130: \]
131: 
132: Integrate first over \(x_j\in[-R,R]\) at fixed remaining coordinates.
133: The fundamental theorem of calculus gives zero because both endpoint
134: values of \(g_j\) are zero. Fubini applies on \(Q\) because the
135: derivative and its two summands are continuous and bounded on a
136: finite-measure box. Thus \(\int_Q\partial_{x_j}g_j=0\).
137: All these terms vanish outside \(Q\), so
138: 
139: \[
140: \int_{\mathbb R^n}\partial_{x_j}u\cdot\partial_{x_j}u_t\,dx
141: =-\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_t\cdot\partial_{x_jx_j}u\,dx.              \tag{4}
142: \]
143: 
144: Every integral is finite by step 2. Sum (4) over the finitely many
145: spatial indices and substitute (2) into (3):
146: 
147: \[
148: \begin{aligned}
149: E'(t_0)
150: &=2\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_t\cdot u_{tt}\,dx
151:  -2\sum_{j=1}^n\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_t\cdot\partial_{x_jx_j}u\,dx\\
152: &=2\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_t\cdot(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu)\,dx=0,
153: \end{aligned}
154: \]
155: 
156: by (1). This holds at every \(t_0>0\). Hence \(E\) is differentiable
157: with zero derivative on \((0,\infty)\), and is constant there by the
158: mean value theorem. This is conservation of energy with exactly the
159: normalization in the exercise.

1: # Audit B: endpoint fidelity and checked Lean closure
2: 
3: The stage-two policy is `endpoint-fidelity-2` (Audit B schema version 2).
4: Its semantic objects are every original external theorem E and the complete
5: final target P. P includes its parameters, quantifiers, hypotheses, domains and
6: conclusion. Accepted NL0/Audit A remains the source authority; B does not repeat
7: unchanged natural-language proof checking.
8: 
9: ## Normal final acceptance and deviation exception
10: 
11: The normal workflow uses `yui-frozen-interface-acceptance-1`. A complete independent
12: pre-proof review establishes source-to-type fidelity for every E and full P and
13: all definitions needed to interpret them. Final native inspection compares the
14: actual exported full types against that frozen contract, checks the exact defining
15: header/pins and semantic receipt, and validates standalone proof/dependency/trust
16: closure. This normal final gate is pure machine work: no additional final LLM is
17: called. It records inherited semantics, not a newly performed independent Audit B.
18: 
19: The actual E/P types include retained hypotheses and quantifiers. Text labels or
20: a source-hash check alone do not establish this gate. The original mathematical
21: review may be wrong; the machine establishes preservation of that reviewed encoding,
22: not correctness of the reviewer's natural-language judgment.
23: 
24: Only complete proof-integrity success plus genuine endpoint/definition drift may
25: open the exceptional independent B-final review below. A faithful result then has
26: `AUDIT-B-CONDITIONAL`, a freeze-deviation warning and an explicit harness-defect
27: report. Invalid native evidence, incomplete dependencies or changed provenance
28: cannot be overridden semantically. Nonfaithful/unverified results wait for the
29: three explicit user choices in [proof repair](proof-repair.md); accepting a different
30: result does not complete the original target. Explicit/manual legacy semantic
31: receipts remain supported under their original schemas and are not relabeled.
32: Explicitly nonindependent/self-review records remain readable development checks;
33: they cannot grant whole-workflow Audit B acceptance. The same qualification rule
34: applies to supplied Audit A authority and incremental producer/cut reviews.
35: 
36: ## Author correspondence explanations
37: 
38: During interface authoring, provide `endpoint_correspondence`, keyed by every
39: E ID and P. Each entry is `{mode: direct|equivalent, explanation: string}`.
40: Keep it short and useful; do not restate the entire proof or manufacture a
41: line-by-line formalization commentary:
42: 
43: - **Direct:** identify the corresponding variables, hypotheses and assertion.
44:   One sentence is enough when the translation is immediate.
45: - **Equivalent:** explain the mathematical identification or reformulation,
46:   why it works in both directions and which existing conditions it uses.
47:   Point to relevant definitions or checked conversions when needed.
48: 
49: For example, expressing invariance under a finite basis of operators can encode
50: invariance under their linear span: explain the spanning property and closure
51: of a subspace under linear combinations. The review must establish those facts
52: for the actual source algebra/action; the word “equivalent” alone is insufficient.
53: 
54: The postprocessing author carries these notes into each E/P entry in
55: `mapping.json`, checks them against the actual export and completes missing
56: notes for older frozen contracts. It must not change frozen proof statements
57: or bodies merely to improve a note. An explanation is an author's claim, not
58: an Audit B verdict or a formal proof.
59: 
60: ## Semantic responsibility before freeze or at explicit B-final
61: 
62: Read the explanation together with the original source statement and actual
63: elaborated Lean type. Follow the definitions needed to interpret the endpoint,
64: including structure fields that might hide extra assumptions. Check each E/P
65: row, then these four global checks:
66: 
67: 1. `endpoint_inventory_and_scope`: all original E statements and P are covered;
68:    the source version, reviewer scope and inherited qualifications are explicit.
69: 2. `external_statement_fidelity`: each external assumption has the source's
70:    complete mathematical meaning, including conditions and quantifiers. With
71:    no external inputs, record that fact.
72: 3. `complete_target_and_representations`: the entire target theorem has the
73:    same meaning, including every hypothesis. Validate the explanation of each
74:    direct or equivalent encoding and relevant edge cases.
75: 4. `kernel_closure_and_trust`: the actual exported proof compiled, all required
76:    producers and intermediate library ports were discharged, and the checked
77:    root has only the declared external assumptions and permitted foundations.
78: 
79: Equivalent formulations are allowed. Do not reject a faithful encoding because
80: it lacks a particular Mathlib type/name, a separate object for every NL0
81: D node, or a duplicate formal representation. A mathematical source-to-code
82: identification can be checked semantically without constructing an unnecessary
83: second model. If the implementation actually crosses two different Lean
84: representations, the required conversion must occur in checked Lean code.
85: Unexplained equivalence, stronger assumptions, missing hypotheses, changed
86: domains or hidden target assumptions remain defects.
87: 
88: Do not accept an explanation on trust or copy the author's conclusion into the
89: review. Record PASS/FAIL/UNVERIFIED with specific findings and source/type/note
90: locations. A compiler pass cannot substitute for this independent judgment.
